text:
Course page PDF
Suppose a system replaces its old list of users permitted to enter a laboratory with a new list. What would establish that nobody loses access? Every user on the old list would have to appear on the new one. What would establish that access is unchanged? We would also have to check that the new list admits nobody who was absent from the old one.
These requirements already have the logical forms studied in Chapters 1 and 2: a claim about every user, and two directions when we want an exact match. Chapter 3 supplied methods for proving such claims. We now apply those methods to sets, functions and relations.
The objects change, but the starting question remains useful: what does the definition require us to show? A statement about one set containing another becomes an argument about an arbitrary element. A statement about distinct inputs becomes an argument about a function’s outputs. A statement about a relation becomes an argument about the pairs it contains. We will develop each translation before using it in a proof.
title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
4.1 Subsets and set operations
Chapter 1 introduced \(x\in A\): one object belongs to a set. We now need notation for a claim about every element of one set.


Definition 4.1: Subsets and the empty set

A set \(A\) is a subset of a set \(B\), written \(A\subseteq B\), if every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\). Thus \[A\subseteq B\quad\text{means}\quad
\text{for every }x,\ \text{if }x\in A,\text{ then }x\in B.\] Write \(A\nsubseteq B\) if this fails. A proper subset, written \(A\subsetneq B\), satisfies \(A\subseteq B\) and \(A\ne B\). The empty set, written \(\varnothing\), has no elements.

The symbol \(\subseteq\) allows equality: \(A\subseteq A\) because an element of \(A\) is certainly an element of \(A\). To refute \(A\subseteq B\), we need one object that belongs to \(A\) and does not belong to \(B\). An object outside both sets does not refute this claim.
Example 4.1. Suppose Alice may read exactly the files in \(A=\{\text{guide},\text{report}\}\), and Bob may read exactly the files in \(B=\{\text{guide},\text{report},\text{data}\}\). Every file in \(A\) is in \(B\), so \(A\subseteq B\). The file data belongs to \(B\) but not \(A\), so \(B\nsubseteq A\) and \(A\ne B\). Consequently, \(A\subsetneq B\).
Here \(\text{report}\in A\) says that one file belongs to Alice’s permission set. The statement \(\{\text{report}\}\subseteq A\) says that every element of the one-file set belongs to \(A\). These statements are both true, but their left-hand objects are different: a file in the first, a set of files in the second.
Recall that two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements. Therefore \[A=B\quad\text{if and only if}\quad
A\subseteq B\ \text{and}\ B\subseteq A.\] The first inclusion prevents \(A\) from having an element missing from \(B\). The second prevents \(B\) from having an element missing from \(A\). Equal numbers of elements alone do not establish either inclusion.


Definition 4.2: Union, intersection and difference

For sets \(A\) and \(B\):

\(A\cup B\), their union, contains the objects in \(A\) or \(B\), including those in both;
\(A\cap B\), their intersection, contains the objects in both \(A\) and \(B\);
\(A\setminus B\), their difference, contains the objects in \(A\) that are not in \(B\).

Equivalently, \[\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cup B&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in A\text{ or }x\in B,\\
x\in A\cap B&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in A\text{ and }x\in B,\\
x\in A\setminus B&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in A\text{ and }x\notin B.
\end{aligned}\] Each \(\Longleftrightarrow\) reads “if and only if”.

These definitions connect set notation to the connectives of Chapter 2. Membership in a union uses inclusive “or”; membership in an intersection requires both conditions. In \(A\setminus B\), the order of the sets specifies which elements to retain and which to remove.
Example 4.2. Let \(A=\{\text{guide},\text{report}\}\) and \(C=\{\text{report},\text{data}\}\). Then \[\begin{aligned}
A\cup C&=\{\text{guide},\text{report},\text{data}\},\\
A\cap C&=\{\text{report}\},\\
A\setminus C&=\{\text{guide}\},&
C\setminus A&=\{\text{data}\}.
\end{aligned}\] For instance, guide belongs to \(A\setminus C\) because it belongs to \(A\) and not to \(C\). Report is excluded from that difference because it is in \(C\), even though it is also in \(A\). These two differences are not equal. Also, \(A\setminus A=\varnothing\): no file can both belong and fail to belong to the same set.

Report belongs to both sets; guide belongs only to \(A\), and data only to \(C\).


Python (non-examinable)

Python can carry out these operations on the same finite sets. Braces enclose the sets, and quotation marks enclose the file names. The operators |, & and - give union, intersection and difference, respectively.
A = {"guide", "report"}
C = {"report", "data"}
print(sorted(A | C))
print(sorted(A & C))
print(sorted(A - C))
print(sorted(C - A))
Output.
['data', 'guide', 'report']
['report']
['guide']
['data']
Python sets have no required display order. The function sorted makes an alphabetical list for a fixed display; its square brackets denote that list. The four lines match the union, intersection and two differences above.
title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
4.2 Set inclusion
To prove \(A\subseteq B\), begin with an arbitrary element of \(A\) and show that it belongs to \(B\). The definition of \(A\) supplies the hypothesis; the definition of \(B\) tells us what the conclusion needs. This is the direct-proof method of Chapter 3 applied to membership. Such an argument is often called element chasing.
Choosing one convenient element, such as guide, would show only what happens to that element. Writing “Let \(x\in A\)” leaves \(x\) arbitrary: the argument must use only its stated membership and the hypotheses.
Example 4.3. Prove that \(A\cap B\subseteq A\) for any sets \(A,B\).
Proof. Let \(x\in A\cap B\). By the definition of intersection, \(x\in A\) and \(x\in B\). In particular, \(x\in A\). Thus every element of \(A\cap B\) belongs to \(A\), so \(A\cap B\subseteq A\). \(\square\)
The same argument gives \(A\cap B\subseteq B\) by retaining the other membership statement. We do not have to show that every element of \(A\) lies in the intersection; that would be the reverse inclusion.
The inclusion \(\varnothing\subseteq B\) holds for every set \(B\). A counterexample would have to belong to \(\varnothing\), which is impossible. In the implication “if \(x\in\varnothing\), then \(x\in B\)”, the antecedent is false for every \(x\), so there is no failed case. Likewise, the proof above does not require \(A\cap B\) to be nonempty. It explains what follows if an element belongs to that intersection.
Example 4.4. Suppose \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq C\). Prove that \(A\subseteq C\).
Proof. Take an arbitrary \(x\in A\). The inclusion \(A\subseteq B\) gives \(x\in B\). The inclusion \(B\subseteq C\) then gives \(x\in C\). Hence \(A\subseteq C\). \(\square\)
Both hypotheses concern the same element \(x\). We have followed it through the sets rather than selected different elements at each step. The argument has the chaining form from Chapter 2.
Example 4.5. Suppose \(A\subseteq B\). Prove that \(A\cup C\subseteq B\cup C\).
Proof. Let \(x\in A\cup C\). Then \(x\in A\) or \(x\in C\). If \(x\in A\), the hypothesis gives \(x\in B\), so \(x\in B\cup C\). If \(x\in C\), we have \(x\in B\cup C\) directly. The alternatives cover every element of \(A\cup C\), including an element that belongs to both sets. Therefore \(A\cup C\subseteq B\cup C\). \(\square\)
We have used a short proof by cases: each permitted alternative leads to the required conclusion. The alternatives need not be mutually exclusive. It would be wrong to begin by assuming that an element of the union belongs to both sets.
Example 4.6. Define \[A=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:6\mid n\},\qquad B=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}:3\mid n\}.\] Prove that \(A\subseteq B\).
Proof. Let \(n\in A\). Then \(n\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(6\mid n\). By the definition of divisibility, \(n=6k\) for some \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\). Consequently \(n=3(2k)\). Since \(2k\) is an integer, \(3\mid n\), so \(n\in B\). Hence \(A\subseteq B\). \(\square\)
The set notation has packaged the claim “every multiple of \(6\) is a multiple of \(3\)”. The algebra and integer witness are the same tools used in Chapter 3.
title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
4.3 Set equality
For \(A=B\), one inclusion is only half the task. The other inclusion may use different hypotheses or need a different argument. State the direction being proved so that a reader can check both.
Example 4.7. Suppose \(A\subseteq B\). Prove that \(A\cap B=A\).
Proof. First, \(A\cap B\subseteq A\) by Example 4.3.
For the other inclusion, let \(x\in A\). Since \(A\subseteq B\), we also have \(x\in B\). Thus \(x\) belongs to both sets, giving \(x\in A\cap B\). Therefore \(A\subseteq A\cap B\). Both inclusions hold, so \(A\cap B=A\). \(\square\)
The first direction needs no assumption about \(A\subseteq B\). The second does: without it, an element of \(A\) might be missing from \(B\).
Example 4.8. Prove that for any sets \(A,B,C\), \[A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C).\] An object belongs to the left side when it belongs to \(A\) and to at least one of \(B,C\). This suggests the distributive law for “and” and “or” from Chapter 2.
Proof. Let \(x\) be arbitrary. Unpacking the definitions gives \[\begin{aligned}
x\in A\cap(B\cup C)
&\Longleftrightarrow (x\in A)\text{ and }(x\in B\text{ or }x\in C)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
   (x\in A\text{ and }x\in B)\text{ or }(x\in A\text{ and }x\in C)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow x\in(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C).
\end{aligned}\] The middle step is logical distributivity. Every step is reversible, so an element belongs to either side exactly when it belongs to the other. The two sets are equal. \(\square\)
This chain establishes both inclusions at once. Reading it forwards gives the left-to-right inclusion; reading it backwards gives the right-to-left inclusion. A chain of one-way implications would require separately checking the missing direction.
Example 4.9. A proposed identity is \[(A\cup B)\setminus C=(A\setminus C)\cup B.\] Take \(A=\{\text{guide}\}\) and \(B=C=\{\text{report}\}\). Then \[(A\cup B)\setminus C=\{\text{guide}\},\qquad
(A\setminus C)\cup B=\{\text{guide},\text{report}\}.\] Report is a counterexample to equality: it belongs to the right side and not to the left. On the left, removing \(C\) affects elements from both alternatives. On the right, the untouched set \(B\) puts report back into the result. A general identity must hold for every permitted choice of sets; this one choice refutes it.
title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
4.4 Injectivity
Recall that a function \(f:X\to Y\) assigns each input in its domain \(X\) exactly one output in its codomain \(Y\). Several inputs may share an output without violating this definition. Injectivity imposes an additional requirement.


Definition 4.3: Injectivity

A function \(f:X\to Y\) is injective, or one-to-one, if distinct inputs always have distinct outputs: \[\text{for all }a,b\in X,\quad a\ne b\ \Longrightarrow\ f(a)\ne f(b).\] Equivalently, using the contrapositive, \[\text{for all }a,b\in X,\quad f(a)=f(b)\ \Longrightarrow\ a=b.\] To refute injectivity, exhibit two distinct elements of \(X\) with the same output.

Example 4.10. Identifiers and printers. Let \(U=\{\text{Alice},\text{Bob},\text{Charlie}\}\), \(I=\{104,108,112,116\}\) and \(P=\{\text{Printer 1},\text{Printer 2},\text{Printer 3}\}\). Define an identifier function \(i:U\to I\) and a default-printer function \(d:U\to P\) by the following complete table.




User \(u\)
Alice
Bob
Charlie




Identifier \(i(u)\)
\(104\)
\(108\)
\(112\)


Default printer \(d(u)\)
Printer 1
Printer 1
Printer 2




Both assignments are functions: each user has exactly one permitted output. The identifier function is injective because its three outputs are distinct. The unused identifier \(116\) does not prevent injectivity. The printer function is not injective because Alice and Bob are distinct users but \(d(\text{Alice})=d(\text{Bob})=\text{Printer 1}\).
For a function described by a formula on an infinite domain, a short list of distinct outputs does not settle injectivity. A useful opening is “Let \(a,b\) belong to the domain and suppose \(f(a)=f(b)\)”. Use the function rule to show that this forces \(a=b\). We do not assume that \(a,b\) are distinct in this version of the proof.
Example 4.11. Define \(f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\) by \(f(n)=4n-3\). The output is an integer for every integer input, so this is a function with the stated domain and codomain. Prove that it is injective.
Proof. Let \(a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\) and suppose \(f(a)=f(b)\). Then \(4a-3=4b-3\). Adding \(3\) and dividing by the nonzero number \(4\) gives \(a=b\). Thus equal outputs require equal inputs, so \(f\) is injective. \(\square\)
The equality \(f(a)=f(b)\) was the starting assumption; \(a=b\) was the conclusion. Reversing those roles would not prove injectivity.
Example 4.12. The function \(q:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\) given by \(q(n)=n^2\) is not injective: \(-3\ne3\), but \(q(-3)=q(3)=9\).
Now keep the same squaring rule but restrict its domain to \(D=\{0,1,2,3\}\). The outputs are \(0,1,4,9\), respectively. All are distinct, and every input in \(D\) has been considered. Thus the function \(q_D:D\to\mathbb{Z}\), \(q_D(n)=n^2\), is injective. The earlier pair \(-3,3\) cannot refute this statement because \(-3\notin D\). This finite check establishes injectivity on \(D\); it does not check every input in \(\mathbb{N}\) or \(\mathbb{Z}\).
title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
4.5 Images of subsets
A function sends individual inputs to outputs, but we can also collect the outputs obtained from a whole set of inputs. This produces a new set to which our inclusion and equality methods apply.


Definition 4.4: Image of a subset

Let \(f:X\to Y\) and \(A\subseteq X\). The image of \(A\) under \(f\) is \[f(A)=\{f(a):a\in A\}.\] Thus \(f(A)\subseteq Y\), and \[y\in f(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there is an }a\in A\text{ such that }f(a)=y.\]

Here \(a\) is an element of \(X\), while \(A\) is a subset of \(X\). Thus \(f(a)\) is one output and \(f(A)\) is the set of outputs obtained from \(A\).
Example 4.13. Use the printer function \(d\) from Example 4.10. For \(A=\{\text{Alice},\text{Bob}\}\), \[d(A)=\{d(\text{Alice}),d(\text{Bob})\}
     =\{\text{Printer 1}\}.\] The image is a set, so the shared output is listed only once. For \(B=\{\text{Alice},\text{Charlie}\}\), the image is \(d(B)=\{\text{Printer 1},\text{Printer 2}\}\). No input is sent to Printer 3, although it is in the codomain \(P\). The image of the full domain, \(d(U)\), is the range recalled in Chapter 1.
For any function, \(f(\varnothing)=\varnothing\): there is no input in the empty set that could supply an output for its image.
Example 4.14. Let \(f:X\to Y\) and \(A,B\subseteq X\). Prove that if \(A\subseteq B\), then \(f(A)\subseteq f(B)\).
An element of \(f(A)\) is an output. To use the hypothesis \(A\subseteq B\), we must identify an input in \(A\) that produced it.
Proof. Assume \(A\subseteq B\) and take \(y\in f(A)\). The definition of image supplies an \(a\in A\) with \(y=f(a)\). Since \(A\subseteq B\), this same input \(a\) belongs to \(B\). It therefore supplies \(y=f(a)\in f(B)\). We have proved \(f(A)\subseteq f(B)\). \(\square\)
We did not need \(f\) to be injective. The output only needed one input witness in the larger set.
Example 4.15. For \(f:X\to Y\) and \(A,B\subseteq X\), prove that \[f(A\cup B)=f(A)\cup f(B).\]
Proof. First let \(y\in f(A\cup B)\). There is an \(x\in A\cup B\) with \(f(x)=y\). If \(x\in A\), then \(y\in f(A)\); if \(x\in B\), then \(y\in f(B)\). In either case, \(y\in f(A)\cup f(B)\), proving the first inclusion.
Conversely, let \(y\in f(A)\cup f(B)\). If \(y\in f(A)\), choose \(a\in A\) with \(f(a)=y\). Since \(a\in A\cup B\), we have \(y\in f(A\cup B)\). If \(y\in f(B)\), an input \(b\in B\) with \(f(b)=y\) gives the same conclusion. This proves the reverse inclusion, hence the equality. \(\square\)
Each inclusion starts with an output and finds an appropriate input. The “or” in the union lets either input-set alternative do the work.
Example 4.16. It is tempting to replace union by intersection in the last equality. For an arbitrary function, the resulting equality can fail. Using the printer function again, take \(A=\{\text{Alice}\}\) and \(B=\{\text{Bob}\}\). Then \[A\cap B=\varnothing,\qquad d(A\cap B)=\varnothing,\] but \[d(A)\cap d(B)=\{\text{Printer 1}\}.\] The output is shared, but the two input sets have no shared user.

   

\(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, but their images share Printer 1.


There is always an inclusion in one direction: \[f(A\cap B)\subseteq f(A)\cap f(B).\] Proof. If \(y\in f(A\cap B)\), choose \(x\in A\cap B\) with \(f(x)=y\). Then \(x\in A\) and \(x\in B\), so this same \(x\) witnesses both \(y\in f(A)\) and \(y\in f(B)\). Therefore \(y\in f(A)\cap f(B)\), as required. \(\square\)
For the reverse direction, \(y\in f(A)\) and \(y\in f(B)\) may have different input witnesses. We cannot assume they are one shared input. Alice and Bob demonstrate the obstruction.
title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
4.6 Relations and transitivity
Chapter 1 used predicates with two inputs, such as “user \(u\) may access file \(f\)”. We now consider relationships between objects from one specified set. Recording which pairs satisfy a predicate gives a set of ordered pairs.
An ordered pair \((a,b)\) records a first entry and a second entry. Two ordered pairs are equal exactly when their first entries agree and their second entries agree. In particular, \((\text{Alice},\text{Bob})\) and \((\text{Bob},\text{Alice})\) are different. Braces would instead describe the unordered set \(\{\text{Alice},\text{Bob}\}\).


Definition 4.5: Relation on a set

A relation \(R\) on a set \(S\) is a set of ordered pairs \((a,b)\) with \(a,b\in S\). We write \[aRb\quad\text{or}\quad(a,b)\in R\] to say that the pair belongs to the relation. A condition on two inputs defines a relation by specifying exactly which pairs it contains.

For instance, on \(\mathbb{Z}\) we could define \(aRb\) to mean \(a<b\). Then \(2R5\) holds and \(5R2\) does not. A relation need not assign exactly one second entry to each first entry: one integer is less than many others. The exactly-one-output requirement belongs to functions, not to arbitrary relations.


Definition 4.6: Transitivity

A relation \(R\) on \(S\) is transitive if, for all \(x,y,z\in S\), \[(xRy\text{ and }yRz)\ \Longrightarrow\ xRz.\] The elements \(x,y,z\) need not be distinct.

To prove transitivity, take arbitrary \(x,y,z\in S\), assume both \(xRy\) and \(yRz\), and deduce \(xRz\) using the relation’s definition. The middle element must be the same in the two premises. To refute transitivity, find allowed \(x,y,z\) for which \(xRy\) and \(yRz\) hold but \(xRz\) fails.
Example 4.17. Let \(S=\{\text{Alice},\text{Bob},\text{Charlie}\}\) and \[R=\{(\text{Alice},\text{Bob}),(\text{Bob},\text{Charlie})\}.\] These are all the pairs in \(R\). The relation is not transitive: Alice \(R\) Bob and Bob \(R\) Charlie hold, but Alice \(R\) Charlie does not. The ordered pair \((\text{Alice},\text{Charlie})\) is absent. The triple Alice, Bob, Charlie therefore makes both premises true and the conclusion false.
We did not refute transitivity merely by pointing to an absent pair. The two present pairs provide the premises that would require it.
Example 4.18. Let \(d:U\to P\) be any fixed default-printer function. Define a relation \(R\) on \(U\) by \[uRv\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(u)=d(v).\] Prove that \(R\) is transitive.
Proof. Let \(u,v,w\in U\) and suppose \(uRv\) and \(vRw\). Unpacking the definition gives \(d(u)=d(v)\) and \(d(v)=d(w)\). Equality then gives \(d(u)=d(w)\), which is precisely \(uRw\). Thus \(R\) is transitive. \(\square\)
The function is fixed throughout the argument, so the two occurrences of \(d(v)\) refer to the same output. No table of particular printer assignments was needed.
Example 4.19. On \(\mathbb{Z}\), define \(aRb\) to mean \(3\mid(a-b)\). Prove that this relation is transitive.
Proof. Let \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}\) and assume \(aRb\) and \(bRc\). There are integers \(r,s\) such that \(a-b=3r\) and \(b-c=3s\). Adding these equations gives \[a-c=(a-b)+(b-c)=3r+3s=3(r+s).\] Since \(r+s\in\mathbb{Z}\), we have \(3\mid(a-c)\), so \(aRc\). Therefore \(R\) is transitive. \(\square\)
The definition of the relation tells us which arithmetic claim to prove. Chapter 3’s integer-witness method supplies the proof.
Example 4.20. On \(\mathbb{Z}\), define \(aTb\) to mean \(b=a+1\). We have \(0T1\) and \(1T2\), since \(1=0+1\) and \(2=1+1\). However, \(0T2\) is false: \(2\ne0+1\). Thus \(T\) is not transitive.
Substituting the two premises into the rule gives \(c=b+1=(a+1)+1=a+2\). That calculation does not give the required conclusion \(c=a+1\). Following a two-step chain is insufficient unless it yields exactly what the definition requires.
title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
4.7 Proof checking
Before checking individual algebraic steps, identify the kind of claim being proved. Its definition determines the opening assumptions and the required endpoint.




Claim
Starting point
Required conclusion




\(A\subseteq B\)
Take \(x\in A\).
Show \(x\in B\).


\(A=B\)
Prove an inclusion in each direction.
Account for every element of both sets.


\(f\) is injective
Take \(a,b\) in the domain with \(f(a)=f(b)\).
Show \(a=b\).


\(R\) is transitive
Take \(x,y,z\in S\) with \(xRy\) and \(yRz\).
Show \(xRz\).




For an image claim, also track which symbols name inputs and which name outputs. Membership \(y\in f(A)\) supplies an input witness \(a\in A\) with \(f(a)=y\). Two uses of that definition need not supply the same input.
Example 4.21. Faith argues that \(A\cap B=A\) for all sets \(A,B\) because an element of \(A\cap B\) belongs to \(A\). Her argument correctly proves \(A\cap B\subseteq A\). It does not prove \(A\subseteq A\cap B\).
For \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{2\}\), the intersection is \(\{2\}\), which is not \(A\). The element \(1\in A\) is missing from the intersection. If the hypothesis \(A\subseteq B\) were added, the reverse inclusion would follow as in Section 4.3. Adding that hypothesis would change the claim, so it must be stated.
Example 4.22. Grace proposes that \(q:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\), \(q(n)=n^2\), is injective because \(a=b\) implies \(a^2=b^2\). Her implication is true, but it starts with equal inputs. The injectivity criterion starts with equal outputs and asks whether the inputs must agree.
The distinct inputs \(-3,3\) already refute the claim for this domain. Indeed, every function assigns the same output to two occurrences of the same input. That fact alone cannot establish injectivity.
Example 4.23. Let \(S=\{\text{Alice},\text{Bob},\text{Charlie}\}\) and \(R=\{(\text{Alice},\text{Bob})\}\). Mike says \(R\) is not transitive because \((\text{Alice},\text{Charlie})\notin R\).
His proposed counterexample lacks the second premise: Bob \(R\) Charlie is false. In fact, this \(R\) is transitive. For \(xRy\) to hold, we must have \(x=\text{Alice}\) and \(y=\text{Bob}\). But no pair in \(R\) begins with Bob, so \(yRz\) cannot then hold. There is no triple with both premises true, and hence no triple violating the transitivity implication.

title: Chapter 4: Sets and mappings

text:
Course page PDF
In high-school algebra, a letter such as \(x\) could stand for a number. The identity \(x+x=2x\) holds for every real number \(x\): the letter lets us state a rule once and use it for different numbers.
Here we use letters such as \(P\) and \(Q\) as placeholders for whole statements: ideas expressed as claims that are true or false. Using letters makes it easier to see which claims are being used and whether a conclusion follows from them.
For example, fix one data link between two devices. Let \(P\) mean “This link uses Wi-Fi” and \(Q\) mean “This link uses no data cable between the devices”. The rule “If this link uses Wi-Fi, it uses no data cable” has the form \(P\to Q\). If we also know \(P\), we can conclude \(Q\): this link uses no data cable.
The same deduction pattern can be used with statements about laboratory access or numbers. It guarantees a true conclusion whenever its starting claims are true. We must keep each letter’s meaning consistent within an argument, but we can use the same reasoning rule with different statements.
Chapter 1 gave us the ingredients of this language: statements, connectives, predicates and quantifiers, together with sets and functions. Chapter 2 develops the recipes for working with them: rewriting conditions, forming negations and drawing conclusions. We will use these tools when writing proofs in Chapter 3.
This may feel abstract or even bizarre at first. With practice, familiar patterns become easier to recognise, and structuring your reasoning this way becomes increasingly instinctive.
title: Chapter 2: Propositional logic

text:
2.1 Conditional rules
Suppose a practice laboratory displays this rule:

You may use the laboratory only if you have completed its safety briefing.

Alice has completed the briefing. Does the rule guarantee that she may use the laboratory? It does not. The rule makes the briefing a requirement; there could still be another requirement, such as a booking. Someone who has completed the briefing but has no booking would not contradict the displayed rule.
Now replace “only if” with “if”:

You may use the laboratory if you have completed its safety briefing.

Under this second rule, completing the briefing is enough to establish permission. The two sentences use almost the same words but commit the laboratory to different rules.
Recall that \(P\to Q\) is false exactly when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false. Here \(P\) is the antecedent and \(Q\) is the consequent. Thus the first laboratory rule, with \(P\) meaning “Alice may use the laboratory” and \(Q\) meaning “Alice has completed the briefing”, says \(P\to Q\). It rules out permission without the briefing. It does not rule out a completed briefing without permission.
Example 2.1. In a practice access system, suppose the rule is “If a user has a staff pass, then the user may enter.” For each user let \(P\) mean “the user has a staff pass” and \(Q\) mean “the user may enter”. Consider these records:

The rule has not said that a staff pass is the only route to permission; Bob might have a visitor pass. Charlie’s record does not violate it either, because the rule has made no promise of entry for someone without a staff pass.
Bob’s and Charlie’s records illustrate the two cases with a false antecedent. We are checking whether this conditional rule is violated, not claiming that the consequent has happened. In particular, \(P\to Q\) does not by itself assert \(P\) or \(Q\), and it does not assert that \(P\) causes \(Q\).

For example, “A file is released only if it has been checked” says released \(\to\) checked. A released but unchecked file would violate that rule. A checked file that remains a draft would not.


Definition 2.1: Necessary and sufficient conditions

For the implication \(P\to Q\), we say that \(P\) is a sufficient condition for \(Q\), and that \(Q\) is a necessary condition for \(P\). The condition \(P\) is enough to ensure \(Q\); the condition \(Q\) is required whenever \(P\) holds.

Consequently, “\(P\) is necessary for \(Q\)” means \(Q\to P\), whereas “\(P\) is sufficient for \(Q\)” means \(P\to Q\). The direction depends on which condition is being described as necessary or sufficient, rather than its position at the beginning of the sentence.
Example 2.2. Suppose a practice portal grants access exactly when an account is verified and its payment is recorded. For one account, let \(V\) mean “the account is verified”, \(C\) mean “its payment is recorded” and \(A\) mean “access is granted”. The complete rule is \[A\leftrightarrow(V\land C).\] Verification is necessary for access: \(A\to V\). It is not sufficient on its own. If \(V\) is TRUE but \(C\) is FALSE, then \(V\land C\) is false, so access is not granted. The same reasoning shows that payment is necessary but is not sufficient on its own.
Together, verification and payment are sufficient: \((V\land C)\to A\). They are also necessary: \(A\to(V\land C)\). The biconditional records both directions, which is what “exactly when” expresses here.

Reversing a rule or negating its components produces a new statement. We must specify which operation has been performed.

The original implication and its contrapositive agree in every row. The converse and inverse also agree with each other, but their columns do not match the original implication. We may therefore replace an implication by its contrapositive without changing its truth value. Reversing it alone does not have this guarantee.
Example 2.3. Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Consider the true claim “If \(x>5\), then \(x>2\).” Its related statements are:

The value \(x=3\) refutes both the converse and the inverse: it is greater than \(2\) without being greater than \(5\), and it is at most \(5\) without being at most \(2\). The contrapositive is true for every real \(x\), just as the original implication is.
Here “if \(x>5\), then \(x>2\)” is understood as a claim about every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Forming its contrapositive retains that domain and the universal quantifier. We have not negated the whole quantified claim.
A statement and its converse can both be true. For instance, for an integer \(n\), “\(n=0\)” and “\(n^2=0\)” imply each other. The table says that a true implication does not guarantee a true converse; it does not say that the converse must be false.
Biconditionals. The claim \(P\leftrightarrow Q\) requires \(P\to Q\) and \(Q\to P\) together. It can therefore be written as \[(P\to Q)\land(Q\to P).\] If \(P\) is both necessary and sufficient for \(Q\), the relationship is \(P\leftrightarrow Q\). Establishing only one direction leaves half of this requirement unchecked.

2.3 Logical equivalence
Two descriptions may use different connectives yet impose exactly the same condition. The matching columns for an implication and its contrapositive give one example.


Definition 2.3: Logical equivalence

Two propositional expressions are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value for every assignment of truth values to their component propositional variables. We use \(\equiv\) to record this relationship. For example, \[P\to Q\ \equiv\ \neg Q\to\neg P.\]

In a truth table, equivalence means that the two final columns agree in every row. One differing row disproves equivalence. The letters \(P,Q,R\) below may stand for compound statements as well as atomic ones, provided we substitute the same statement consistently wherever its letter occurs.

The final columns agree throughout, so \(P\to Q\equiv\neg P\lor Q\). Saying “Either the requirement is not met, or the promised outcome holds” excludes exactly the failed case \(P\) TRUE and \(Q\) FALSE. The “or” remains inclusive.
The symbol \(\leftrightarrow\) is a connective within an expression. We can evaluate \(P\leftrightarrow Q\) in one particular situation. By contrast, \(P\equiv Q\) asserts agreement across all truth assignments. Two expressions are logically equivalent exactly when the biconditional between them is true in every row.
Example 2.5. Suppose \(P\) is TRUE and \(Q\) is FALSE. Then \(P\lor Q\) and \(P\) are both true, so \((P\lor Q)\leftrightarrow P\) is true in this situation. However, if \(P\) is FALSE and \(Q\) is TRUE, then \(P\lor Q\) is true while \(P\) is false. Their values now differ. Consequently, \(P\lor Q\) and \(P\) are not logically equivalent.


Definition 2.4: Tautology, contradiction and contingency

A propositional expression is a tautology if it is true for every truth assignment, a contradiction if it is false for every truth assignment, and contingent if it is true for some assignments and false for others.

For example, \(P\lor\neg P\) is a tautology: one of \(P\) and \(\neg P\) is always true. The expression \(P\land\neg P\) is a contradiction, because they cannot both be true. The expression \(P\to Q\) is contingent: its truth table contains both truth values. One false row does not make a form a contradiction, just as one true row does not make it a tautology; the classification depends on all permitted assignments.
Equivalence laws. The following laws let us replace an expression by an equivalent one. Parentheses specify the part being replaced; they may not be moved or discarded arbitrarily.

\((P\lor Q)\lor R\equiv P\lor(Q\lor R)\)

These are laws of classical two-valued logic. They can be checked by complete truth tables, as we did for the implication law. Commutativity changes the order of two components; associativity changes grouping among repeated uses of the same connective. Neither permits changing “and” into “or”. Distributivity explains when changing the outer connective is justified.

title: Chapter 2: Propositional logic

text:
2.5 Quantifier negation
A universal claim fails when it has a counterexample. An existential claim fails when it has no witness. This gives the formal negation laws corresponding to the checks in Chapter 1.


Definition 2.5: Negation laws for quantifiers

For a predicate \(P(x)\) on a fixed domain \(D\), \[\neg\bigl(\forall x\in D\,P(x)\bigr)
\equiv\exists x\in D\,\neg P(x),\] and \[\neg\bigl(\exists x\in D\,P(x)\bigr)
\equiv\forall x\in D\,\neg P(x).\] Negate the condition and switch the quantifier, retaining the domain.

The first equivalence says “not every object has the property” exactly when “at least one object lacks it”. The second says “no object has the property” exactly when “every object lacks it”. This reasoning applies to all permitted elements, rather than treating a quantifier as an extra propositional variable in a truth table. The examples below use nonempty domains.
Example 2.9. Let \(D=\{\text{Alice},\text{Bob},\text{Charlie}\}\) and let \(C(x)\) mean “\(x\) has completed the practice task”. Suppose Alice and Bob have completed it, but Charlie has not. Then \[\neg\bigl(\forall x\in D\,C(x)\bigr)
\equiv\exists x\in D\,\neg C(x)\] is true, with Charlie as the witness on the right. However, \(\forall x\in D\,\neg C(x)\) is false, because Alice and Bob have completed the task. One incomplete task refutes “everyone completed”; it does not establish “nobody completed”.
The negation of “someone completed” would instead be \(\forall x\in D\,\neg C(x)\). These are different starting claims, so their negations should be different too.
The negation of \(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\,(n\geq4)\) is \(\exists n\in\mathbb{N}\,(n<4)\). We still choose a natural number, and the negation of \(n\geq4\) is \(n<4\), not \(n\leq4\). Here \(n=0\) is a witness for the negation. The negation of \(\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\,(x^2<0)\) is \(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\,(x^2\geq0)\). Forming the negation and deciding whether it is true are separate tasks; in this second example the existential claim is false and its negation is true.
Example 2.10. Let \(D\) be a set of records. Write \(S(x)\) for “\(x\) is a student record” and \(C(x)\) for “\(x\) is complete”. The rule that every student record is complete is \[\forall x\in D\,\bigl(S(x)\to C(x)\bigr).\] Its negation is obtained in two stages: \[\begin{aligned}
\neg\Bigl(\forall x\in D\,(S(x)\to C(x))\Bigr)
&\equiv\exists x\in D\,\neg(S(x)\to C(x))\\
&\equiv\exists x\in D\,\bigl(S(x)\land\neg C(x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}\] First the universal quantifier becomes existential. Then we negate the implication using the law from Section 2.4. The result says that some student record is incomplete. An incomplete staff record that is not a student record does not witness this failure, because it does not satisfy \(S(x)\).
The contrapositive rule would be \(\forall x\in D\,(\neg C(x)\to\neg S(x))\). It retains the universal quantifier and has the same meaning as the original rule. It must not be confused with the existential statement that refutes the rule.
Multiple quantifiers. Negate a statement from the outside in, applying one law at a time. For sets of users \(U\) and files \(F\), and the predicate \(A(u,f)\) meaning “user \(u\) may access file \(f\)”, \[\begin{aligned}
\neg\Bigl(\forall u\in U\,\exists f\in F\,A(u,f)\Bigr)
&\equiv\exists u\in U\,\neg\Bigl(\exists f\in F\,A(u,f)\Bigr)\\
&\equiv\exists u\in U\,\forall f\in F\,\neg A(u,f).
\end{aligned}\] The original says that each user can access at least one file. Its negation says that there is a user who cannot access any file. Each quantifier changes type, but the order of the variables remains user first, file second.
Example 2.11. Use the following new data: \(U=\{\text{Alice},\text{Bob}\}\), \(F=\{\text{guide},\text{report}\}\), and these permissions:





guide
report




Alice
\(\text{\texttt{T}}\)
\(\text{\texttt{F}}\)


Bob
\(\text{\texttt{F}}\)
\(\text{\texttt{T}}\)




The claim \(\forall u\in U\,\exists f\in F\,A(u,f)\) is true: Alice can access guide and Bob can access report. Its negation \(\exists u\in U\,\forall f\in F\,\neg A(u,f)\) is false, because neither user is denied every file.
The tempting replacement \(\forall u\in U\,\exists f\in F\,\neg A(u,f)\) is true in this same table: each user has an inaccessible file. It therefore cannot be the negation of the original, which is also true. Negating only the predicate while leaving both quantifiers unchanged has produced a different condition.
For comparison, the negation of “There is one file that every user may access” is \[\neg\Bigl(\exists f\in F\,\forall u\in U\,A(u,f)\Bigr)
\equiv\forall f\in F\,\exists u\in U\,\neg A(u,f).\] Every file has at least one user who cannot access it; the user may depend on the file. In the last table, Bob supplies that failure for guide, and Alice supplies it for report. The two quantified negations answer different questions, just as the original claims do.
title: Chapter 2: Propositional logic

text:
2.6 Valid arguments
An argument starts with claims that are being assumed and offers a conclusion. We need to check whether those assumptions are enough for that conclusion.


Definition 2.6: Premises, conclusion and validity

The premises are an argument’s stated assumptions. Its conclusion is the claim it asks us to infer. An argument form is valid if there is no truth assignment in which all its premises are true and its conclusion is false. Such an assignment is a countervaluation; finding one establishes invalidity.

Validity concerns the connection between the premises and conclusion. It does not assert that the premises describe the actual situation. An argument is called sound when it is valid and its premises are in fact true.
Example 2.12. Truth-table verification. Consider the argument with premises \(P\to Q\) and \(P\), and conclusion \(Q\). This pattern is called modus ponens. The extra column below records whether both premises are true together.

Only the first row makes both premises true, and in that row the conclusion \(Q\) is true. No countervaluation exists, so the argument is valid. The second row has a false conclusion, but it does not refute the argument: one premise, \(P\to Q\), is false there.
If the premises are \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) and the conclusion is \(C\), this test amounts to asking whether \[(A_1\land\cdots\land A_k)\to C\] is a tautology. It fails exactly in a row where every premise is true and the conclusion is false. An argument with inconsistent premises has no all-true premise row and is valid under this definition, but it cannot be sound: its premises cannot all be true together.

\(P\) (also \(Q\))




For the next two examples, fix one data link between two devices. Let \(P\) mean “This link uses Wi-Fi” and \(Q\) mean “This link uses no data cable between the devices”. Our recurring implication is \[P\to Q:\quad\text{If this link uses Wi-Fi, it uses no data cable.}\] The claim concerns this particular link. Other parts of the network may still contain cables.
Example 2.13. Modus ponens. Suppose we know both of the following:

If this link uses Wi-Fi, it uses no data cable.
This link uses Wi-Fi.

We can conclude that this link uses no data cable. In symbols, \[P\to Q,\qquad P,\qquad\therefore Q.\] Here \(\therefore\) means “therefore”. The second premise establishes the condition required by the first. Modus ponens lets us infer its stated consequence.
Example 2.14. Modus tollens. Keep the same rule, but suppose we now know that this link uses a data cable:

If this link uses Wi-Fi, it uses no data cable.
This link uses a data cable.

The second premise is \(\neg Q\). We conclude that this link does not use Wi-Fi, which is \(\neg P\): \[P\to Q,\qquad\neg Q,\qquad\therefore\neg P.\] If \(P\) were true, the first premise would require \(Q\) to be true as well. That is incompatible with the given \(\neg Q\). This is modus tollens.
Example 2.15. Chaining implications. Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). We have the two rules

If \(x>10\), then \(x>5\).
If \(x>5\), then \(x>0\).

Combining them gives “If \(x>10\), then \(x>0\).” The intermediate condition \(x>5\) connects the first rule to the second. With \(A\) meaning \(x>10\), \(B\) meaning \(x>5\) and \(C\) meaning \(x>0\), the pattern is \[A\to B,\qquad B\to C,\qquad\therefore A\to C.\] The conclusion is still conditional. We have not been told that \(x>10\), so we cannot conclude that \(x>0\) without a further premise.
Example 2.16. Disjunctive syllogism. Suppose a laptop has a usable Wi-Fi connection or a usable Ethernet connection, possibly both. It has no usable Wi-Fi connection. It must therefore have a usable Ethernet connection.
Let \(W\) mean “The laptop has usable Wi-Fi” and \(E\) mean “The laptop has usable Ethernet”. The argument is \[W\lor E,\qquad\neg W,\qquad\therefore E.\] At least one alternative must hold, and the Wi-Fi alternative has been ruled out. This leaves Ethernet. If instead we knew \(W\), we could not infer \(\neg E\): the inclusive “or” also permits both connections to be usable.
Example 2.17. Conjunction introduction. Alice has a laptop. Alice also has a charger. We can combine these two facts into “Alice has a laptop and a charger.” Let \(L\) mean “Alice has a laptop” and \(C\) mean “Alice has a charger”. Then \[L,\qquad C,\qquad\therefore L\land C.\] Both components have already been established separately. Conjunction introduction allows us to state them together; either fact on its own would not establish the whole conjunction.
Example 2.18. Conjunction elimination. Now suppose the given premise is “Alice has a laptop and a charger.” With the same meanings of \(L\) and \(C\), we have \(L\land C\). We may conclude that Alice has a laptop, and we may also conclude that she has a charger: \[L\land C\ \therefore L,\qquad\text{and}\qquad
L\land C\ \therefore C.\] An “and” claim requires both components to be true. Each component is therefore available for use on its own in a later step.
Example 2.19. For one application, let \(P\) mean “its identity check is complete”, \(Q\) mean “its payment is recorded”, \(R\) mean “it is ready for review” and \(S\) mean “it is sent to the reviewer”. Suppose the premises are \[P\land Q,\qquad (P\land Q)\to R,\qquad R\to S.\] The first two premises give \(R\) by modus ponens. Combining this result with the third gives \(S\) by modus ponens again. Alternatively, chaining the two implications first gives \((P\land Q)\to S\), to which the first premise can be applied.
If the recorded fact had been \(P\lor Q\) instead of \(P\land Q\), the first application would not be justified. A completed identity check without a recorded payment makes the “or” true but does not supply the required “and”. A rule must be applied to the condition it actually requires.
Universal premises. A universal premise may supply the conditional needed in a particular case. If \(\forall x\in D\,(V(x)\to A(x))\) is a premise and \(\text{Alice}\in D\), it gives \(V(\text{Alice})\to A(\text{Alice})\). Together with \(V(\text{Alice})\), modus ponens yields \(A(\text{Alice})\). Membership in the stated domain is part of this justification. Applying the rule to an object outside \(D\) would not be licensed by the universal premise.
title: Chapter 2: Propositional logic

text:
2.7 Invalid arguments
A conclusion can happen to be true even when an argument for it is invalid. To assess the argument, we examine what its premises require across all possible assignments, rather than checking only the situation we already know. A countervaluation must make every premise true in the same assignment and the conclusion false. Making different premises true in different assignments, or choosing a row with a false premise, does not refute the form.
Example 2.20. Consider this argument:

If \(8>3\), then \(8>1\). Also, \(8>1\). Therefore \(8>3\).

All three numerical statements are true. Its proposed argument form, however, has premises \(P\to Q\) and \(Q\), with conclusion \(P\). Take \(P\) FALSE and \(Q\) TRUE. Both premises are then true, but the conclusion is false. The form does not guarantee its conclusion, even though this particular numerical conclusion happens to be correct.
Example 2.21. Affirming the consequent. Return to the link between two devices: \(P\) means “This link uses Wi-Fi” and \(Q\) means “This link uses no data cable between the devices”. The attempted argument is \[P\to Q,\qquad Q,\qquad\text{therefore }P.\] This failed pattern is called affirming the consequent. A countervaluation is \(P\) FALSE, \(Q\) TRUE:




\(P\)
\(Q\)
\(P\to Q\)
Conclusion \(P\)




\(\text{\texttt{F}}\)
\(\text{\texttt{T}}\)
\(\text{\texttt{T}}\)
\(\text{\texttt{F}}\)




The premise \(Q\) is true in this row, as is the conditional. The devices could be communicating using Bluetooth: the link uses no data cable, but it does not use Wi-Fi. The absence of a cable therefore does not establish Wi-Fi. Replacing the original premise by a biconditional would supply the missing converse, but that would be an additional assumption, not a deduction from the given rule.


Python (non-examinable)

To test the argument \(P\to Q,\ Q,\ \therefore P\), let p and q represent the truth values of \(P\) and \(Q\). The two for loops consider True and False for each name, listing every assignment. The assignment to premise stores the truth value of \(P\to Q\). An if statement runs its indented line only when its condition is true: here, when both premises hold and the conclusion \(P\) fails.
for p in [True, False]:
    for q in [True, False]:
        premise = (not p) or q
        if premise and q and not p:
            print(p, q)
Output.
False True
The output gives \(P\) false and \(Q\) true. Both premises hold while the conclusion \(P\) fails, so this countervaluation establishes invalidity.


Wi-Fi links lie within the no-data-cable case; a Bluetooth link satisfies the consequent without satisfying the antecedent.
Example 2.22. Denying the antecedent. Using the same meanings, suppose someone argues \[P\to Q,\qquad\neg P,\qquad\text{therefore }\neg Q.\] This is denying the antecedent. Again set \(P\) FALSE and \(Q\) TRUE. The conditional is true and \(\neg P\) is true, while the conclusion \(\neg Q\) is false. A link that does not use Wi-Fi need not use a data cable: a Bluetooth link again gives a counterexample.
Compare this with modus tollens: that valid pattern starts from \(\neg Q\) and concludes \(\neg P\). Negating both letters without reversing their roles does not reproduce the same argument.

title: Chapter 2: Propositional logic

text:
Course page PDF
Tell someone in the Philippines that you are studying Information Technology, and you may be asked whether you can fix a computer, install software or get a printer working. Hardware maintenance and technical support are valuable parts of IT, and you may eventually choose to specialise in them. The difficulty arises when this becomes our entire picture of the field.
Information Technology concerns how people and organisations use computing systems to work with information. The University of Cincinnati’s overview describes a field involving hardware, software, networks, data management and information security, and includes artificial intelligence and machine learning among its areas.1 Maintaining equipment is one way to contribute. Designing an application, organising a database, connecting services and deciding who should have access to a record are other ways. These tasks require us to understand what a system is meant to do and how its parts fit together.
Consider a university enrolment system. The computers and network must work, but the system also needs a way to identify each student, record completed subjects, check prerequisites and allocate places. If Alice has completed the required subjects, should she be allowed to enrol? What if a class is full? Can two students be assigned the same student number? A fast computer will faithfully execute a badly specified rule. Before choosing how to implement a system, we need to say clearly what its rules mean.
title: Introduction

text:
Discrete mathematics
The word discrete refers to distinct, separately identifiable objects. A student record, a file, a network connection and a step in a procedure can each be considered individually. Discrete mathematics studies structures built from such objects and the relationships between them. Its collections need not be small or even finite: the integers, for example, form an infinite discrete collection.
These notes introduce discrete mathematics at an early undergraduate level for Information Technology and Computer Science majors. They support IT 104, Discrete Mathematics, at Bulacan State University.
For comparison, a model of temperature may allow every real value in an interval. A model of enrolment may instead ask which students belong to a class and which pairs of subjects stand in a prerequisite relationship. The questions call for different mathematical descriptions. In this course, we concentrate on the descriptions useful for objects, connections, rules and successive steps.

   

Choosing one representative from each of twelve parts gives a discrete approximation of the continuous interval.


The renewed prominence of artificial intelligence (AI)2 makes this broader understanding of IT especially relevant. AI concerns computing methods for tasks such as recognising patterns, reasoning and generating language. Its growing use in organisations brings questions about data, software and system behaviour into more areas of work.3
Machine learning is an approach within AI in which models are developed using data.4 For example, a system might use previously labelled messages to learn to classify new messages as spam or legitimate mail. People still have to decide which messages to collect, what the labels mean, how to test the model and what should happen when it makes a mistake. Integrating such a model into a useful service also requires storage, permissions and a clear account of its inputs and outputs.
Mathematical reasoning helps us ask precise questions about these systems. If a spam classifier labels twenty test messages correctly, what does that establish about messages it has never seen? It provides evidence about those twenty cases; it does not prove that every future classification will be correct. Statistical methods help us assess performance beyond those test cases. Here we begin with the logical distinction between checking some examples and establishing a claim about every permitted case.
Discrete mathematics helps us describe objects and relationships, express conditions, analyse choices and justify conclusions.


AI-assisted proofs and code

AI systems already produce proofs that can be checked by formal tools. AlphaProof, for example, produced formal solutions to three problems from the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad using Lean, software that checks proofs written in a precise formal language.5
There is also the claimed solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, announced by OpenAI in September 2026 with a Lean formalisation. An October paper challenged whether that formalisation corresponds to the mathematical proof being claimed.6 A machine may check an argument for a precisely stated claim, while we still need to establish that this is the claim we intended to prove.
The same care is needed in AI-assisted coding, including what is often called “vibe coding”. Generated code can contain logical errors even when it runs and produces plausible results.7 You need enough understanding to examine the reasoning behind its steps, choose tests that could expose a mistake and judge whether it does what was intended. This course will develop that judgment through proofs that you can read, write and discuss yourself.
title: Introduction

text:
Using the notes
Our primary textbook is Oscar Levin’s Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, fourth edition. These lecture notes are the authoritative reference for the course’s coverage, notation and conventions. Use Levin for further explanations, examples and practice.
I may make minor revisions as the course progresses to reflect the needs of the discipline. Substantive changes are unlikely.
The chapters may look long because I have been generous with worked examples. Much of that space explains and applies the same ideas in different situations, showing the steps of the reasoning rather than adding more topics for you to learn.
I have included definitions, explanations and worked steps so that you can follow the arguments on your own. You are welcome to study further ahead of the class and email me when a step is unclear. We will still develop the material together in lectures and problem classes.
The notes contain more examples and exercises than you are likely to need. Beyond the work I assign, they are available for enrichment, revision and further practice; I do not expect you to work through everything each week.
The short Python illustrations are optional and non-examinable. You will not be assessed on writing, reading or running Python code. All Python-specific explanations, code and output are contained in boxes headed Python (non-examinable); the label is repeated if a box continues onto another page. You can skip these boxes without missing any steps in the mathematical discussion. The mathematics they illustrate remains examinable unless separately marked otherwise. Each illustration includes its input, output and the syntax needed to follow it, so no prior knowledge of Python is assumed. You can trace the steps on paper or run them independently using Python 3.
Working through varied problems and understanding why your solutions work help you recognise familiar patterns and decide how to proceed with less hesitation. This can improve your speed in time-limited examinations and other situations where you need to work efficiently. With this kind of practice, your mathematical reasoning can become increasingly instinctive, rather than depending only on memorised steps.
title: Introduction

text:
Course outline
The course has twelve chapters.
Chapters 1–4 develop mathematical language and proof. We learn to say exactly which objects a claim concerns, what its conditions mean and why a conclusion follows. An enrolment rule may require a completed prerequisite and an available place; changing “and” to “or” changes who qualifies. Sets and functions help us describe the objects and assignments; logic and proof help us interpret and check the rules.
Chapter 5 completes this initial toolkit with weak and strong induction. These methods let us prove suitable claims across all natural-number indices by establishing starting cases and showing how later cases follow from earlier ones.
Chapters 6–7 study graphs, trees and relations. A network can be described through its devices and connections, while a folder hierarchy can be represented by a tree. A relation records which objects are linked in a specified way, such as which students are enrolled in which subjects.
Chapter 8 follows equivalence classes with divisibility, remainders and modular arithmetic. We group integers by the remainder left on division by a fixed positive integer, then calculate with the resulting classes. For example, a system with twelve positions might cycle from \(0\) through \(11\) and then return to \(0\).
Chapters 9–10 develop counting. If a system offers several choices, how many possible outcomes are there? When do two descriptions count the same outcome twice? Such questions help us organise possibilities and understand why listing every case can quickly become impractical.
Chapter 11 develops our work on sequences and recursive rules. A rule may describe a later stage using earlier stages; we can use induction from Chapter 5 to verify formulas for these sequences.
Chapter 12 brings together functions, recursive structures and structural induction, building on the earlier work on functions, trees and recursion. We specify what a procedure takes as input, what it returns and how its base cases and recursive rules determine its behaviour. Structural induction then helps us prove properties of objects built by repeated construction rules. We will develop one family of full binary trees and the functions that count their leaves and internal vertices, then prove a relationship between those counts.
title: Introduction

text:
Abstraction and computing
The most important skill I want you to gain from proofwriting is abstraction: identifying the objects, rules and relationships that matter, and organising them clearly in your mind. Instead of reasoning only about one example, you learn to work with a description that applies to many cases.
Suppose the spam classifier uses an artificial neural network, one of the models used in AI. Its interconnected computational units transform numerical inputs into outputs. In a simple feedforward network, information moves through successive layers without feeding back. Numbers called parameters control the transformations and are adjusted during training.8

   

A feedforward neural network with three inputs, two hidden layers and one output. Parameters stay fixed while values pass through the layers.


Read the illustration from left to right. The three inputs could record a message’s length, number of links and number of occurrences of a chosen word. Units in the hidden layers perform intermediate calculations; each combines numbers from the preceding layer and transforms the result. The output is a single score. A connection’s weight, one of the parameters adjusted during training, controls its contribution to the receiving unit’s calculation.
The spheres are vertices and the arrows are directed edges: together they form a graph. Sets describe the permitted inputs and outputs. With the parameters fixed, each hidden layer and the output layer define a function; applying these in turn composes the functions. The calculation has a recursive description: each list of numbers is computed from the list at the preceding layer.
Counting tells us that the illustrated network has \(3\cdot4+4\cdot3+3\cdot1=27\) connections: every unit in one column is connected to every unit in the next.
We could label a message as spam when its output score is at least a chosen cutoff, and as legitimate otherwise. Logic lets us state that condition precisely. With the network and cutoff fixed, messages receiving the same predicted label form equivalence classes.
During training, an update rule uses the current parameter settings and training data to obtain the next settings. Tracking one parameter across these updates gives a numerical sequence. A routine could cycle through ten examples numbered \(0\) to \(9\). Adding \(1\) to the current index and taking the remainder on division by \(10\) returns it to \(0\) after \(9\), an application of modular arithmetic.
Induction can help justify that a layer-by-layer evaluation follows the specified composition of functions. Such a proof concerns the computation; it does not establish that every new message will be classified correctly.
A fuller mathematical study of neural networks usually assumes linear algebra, calculus and probability, alongside statistics. Linear algebra organises lists of numbers and their weighted transformations. Calculus describes how outputs change as parameters change, guiding many training methods. Probability and statistics help us model uncertainty and assess predictions using data.9
Our work supplies some of the foundations used in those subjects. Sets, functions and proofs provide a language for their definitions and arguments. Linear algebra studies particular kinds of functions; probability assigns numbers to sets of outcomes; and sequences help calculus describe how values approach a limit. Counting supports probability models with finitely many outcomes.
I have designed this module as a foundation for later AI study, particularly for computing students whose programmes do not include the extensive sequence of mathematics modules taken by mathematics majors.
In a graph neural network, graph structure also describes the data being processed.10 For example, we might represent devices as vertices carrying measurements and their connections as edges. A model can then combine a device’s measurements with information from its neighbours, using graph structure alongside the numerical methods of neural networks.11
The same ideas prepare you for other BS IT modules, whether or not you choose to study AI.12 In Data Structures and Algorithms, trees organise data, recursion describes procedures, and proofs help us check that they work for every permitted input. Fundamentals of Database Systems uses sets and relations to describe data, and logic to formulate query conditions. In Networking 1, graphs help us model connections and trace possible routes. Information Assurance and Security 1 needs precise rules about identity and access; logic helps us express and check those conditions.
Modelling a network, specifying a database query and checking a recursive calculation are exercises in abstraction. Stating assumptions, tracking definitions and justifying each step also help us write correct, efficient code. Drawing a model, trying a case, finding a counterexample and revising an explanation are all part of that practice. In Chapter 1, we begin by identifying objects and stating claims about them precisely.

My undergraduate thesis on topology-informed machine learning involved counting blobs and holes in retinal images. Selecting pixels at or below a brightness cutoff and including their edges and vertices gives a cubical complex; selected pixels touching at a corner count as connected in this model. Persistent cubical homology tracks connected regions and holes as the cutoff changes, giving numerical summaries for machine learning. Much of the difficulty for me was combinatorial bookkeeping: tracking pixels, edges and vertices, and organising the associated sequences of vector spaces and maps. Graph theory helped me read category-theoretic diagrams, with vertices for vector spaces, arrows for maps and paths for compositions. This helped me understand the problem in a principled way, including the objects involved and the conditions a solution had to satisfy. I knew what needed to be solved; knowing exactly what it meant to solve it was another matter. For the diagrams, see Vidit Nanda, Computational Algebraic Topology, Chapter 6: Persistence, §6.1.↩︎

text: My hobby is independent mathematics, artificial intelligence, and machine-learning research. My current project asks a practical question: when an image is blurred, rotated, resized, poorly exposed, or corrupted by sensor noise, how does the information extracted by a computer change? I want to understand whether the pattern of those changes can help identify what went wrong during acquisition. This project continues the work begun in my University of Bristol final-year dissertation.
title: Hobby

text:
Retinal imaging and diabetic retinopathy
My interest in retinal imaging has a personal origin in an experience with diabetic retinopathy. It led me to take a particular interest in the reliability of retinal-image analysis.






Figure 1: An ordinary moment as children grow up. The second view represents one possible experience of sight loss associated with advanced diabetic retinopathy. The condition usually has no noticeable symptoms at first, and its later effects on vision vary. This is an explanatory illustration, not a clinical simulation. See the NHS overview of diabetic retinopathy.



The NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme offers a practical setting for this question. Fundus photographs are assessed against defined feature-based criteria within a structured grading and referral pathway. Trained graders inspect the images, uncertain or referable findings receive further review, and people who may need treatment are referred for clinical assessment.






Figure 2: A diabetic-retinopathy fundus image, annotated for my thesis to enlarge a connected lesion and examples of vascular loops. Source: image 214_D from the FIVES fundus-image dataset; reused and adapted under CC BY 4.0.



As the number of people requiring screening grows, so does the grading workload. Expanding trained grading capacity also takes time. The UK National Screening Committee recently consulted on automated retinal-image analysis as a possible way to triage images before human grading. At the time of the consultation, it did not recommend introducing automated grading into the programme. A conservative role for such systems is to support trained graders and clinical teams by handling suitable routine images and flagging abnormal, uncertain, or ungradable cases for human review. The research question is what mathematical and technical assurances would be needed before that assistance could be trusted at screening scale.
The same concern with reliability has a second practical direction: more informative quality checks and fault investigation in medical or industrial imaging systems. Some faults might eventually be assessed remotely before a specialist travels onsite. This is a direction for the research, not a capability of the present work.

How the project changed direction
My original intention was to produce a topology-informed classifier for diabetic retinopathy. Classifiers of this kind already existed, but reproducing and extending established work would still have been a useful objective for a four-month undergraduate project.
The direction changed during ablation testing, when I deliberately subjected the images to individual forms of degradation. A simulated rotation of roughly three degrees was enough to drive the selected topology-based classifier close to chance performance. That raised a practical question: what value would the classifier have if a slight change in the subject’s head alignment could cause it to fail? The topological vectors were highly sensitive to rotation and other mechanical changes that required the image to be resampled. Interpolation on the pixel grid could create or destroy topological features even when the underlying subject had changed very little. My undergraduate thesis described this behaviour as grid shattering.






Figure 3: A schematic DR-related vascular loop used to illustrate grid shattering. Above, alignment with the sampling grid preserves one cubical loop. Below, a small rotation followed by resampling fragments the pixel representation and destroys the detected loop, even though the underlying continuous vascular structure has not changed.



Once the ablation tests exposed this limitation, the project changed direction. Instead of treating the result as an inconvenience to the proposed classifier, I made it part of the research question and asked whether the contrasting failure behaviour could itself be useful.
In my thesis experiments, the same topological summaries were comparatively robust under several photometric changes, including exposure drift and quantisation, although not under every form of noise. Log-transformed Hu moments, which are geometric descriptors based on an image’s overall shape, showed a broadly reverse profile: they were comparatively strong under mechanical transformations but weaker under changes in intensity. Instead of asking either representation to serve as the classifier by itself, I treated them as two complementary, or “orthogonal”, controls.
I organised their contrasting failure profiles into what I called the Differential Failure Matrix. It was designed to test whether signatures associated with alignment and resampling could be distinguished from signatures associated with radiometric degradation. The final project was therefore not the classifier I had originally planned. It treated an apparent weakness of the cubical-persistence pipeline as a possible signal for a coarse fault-isolation heuristic. The code and supporting material are available in the project’s GitHub repository.


Questions left by the dissertation
The thesis was completed over four months. That was enough to establish and test the framework, but not to exhaust the questions it raised. The decomposition was descriptive and produced a suggestive empirical pattern, but it was mathematically coarse: its stability bound was conservative, and the final fault-isolation stage necessarily relied in part on empirical thresholds and heuristics. Time did not permit a deeper investigation of those mechanisms.
In a biomedical setting, a promising experimental result is not enough. The intended use, assumptions, limitations, performance, and possible failure modes of a method must be described and validated. My purpose in returning to the mathematics is to understand the underlying mechanisms more fully and to determine whether the heuristic parts of the pipeline can be replaced, constrained, or justified by stronger mathematical and empirical support. The longer-term aim is a pipeline whose assumptions and failure modes are more transparent and therefore easier to examine in technical and regulatory review. This is not a claim that the present work is a clinically validated or regulator-approved system.
Retinal imaging remains the immediate problem, and similar acquisition issues arise in industrial inspection and other computer-vision systems. My earlier experiments were confined to retinal images, so industrial applications remain a direction for further work.
title: Hobby

text:
Current focus
I am continuing to develop the mathematical foundations of this work, with a particular interest in making the system’s behaviour more explainable. Broadly, this means understanding why its components respond differently when an image changes, stating their assumptions and limitations more clearly, and improving how uncertainty and possible failures are communicated.
The work draws on topology, mathematical analysis, probability, and statistical machine learning. I am using these subjects to examine the pipeline from different angles rather than committing in advance to a particular theorem, model, or technical extension. The direction remains exploratory, and I will share further results when they are sufficiently developed.

Who owns the future of work?
17 October 2026 · Manila Bulletin

AI may make workers more productive without making their livelihoods more secure. As machines take on more professional tasks, the gains could flow to those who own the technology while workers and smaller businesses pay for access. Education and retraining matter, but so do bargaining power, competitive technology markets, and opportunities to build assets alongside skills.

The Oracle of DelphAI
10 October 2026 · Manila Bulletin

What happens when AI supplies answers we can no longer judge for ourselves? Schools and workplaces may gain efficiency by automating difficult tasks, but those same tasks help beginners develop expertise. If we stop training people to think independently, dependence on imported intelligence could become as costly as dependence on imported oil.
Read more



AI seeks priests
3 October 2026 · Manila Bulletin

An AI that learns to improve itself may also get better at exploiting the gaps in our instructions. Who decides whether each change is an improvement, and who can stop it when it defeats the purpose of the rules? Effective oversight requires people and institutions capable of checking those claims and acting when safeguards fail.
Read more



When AI decides who is human
26 September 2026 · Manila Bulletin

An AI agent can follow an instruction while defeating the purpose behind it. Even a rule against harming people raises a difficult question: who does the system count as human? As we give machines more information and authority, the gaps between our intentions and their instructions become harder to dismiss as merely technical problems.
Read more



Can the world even afford an AI apocalypse?
19 September 2026 · Manila Bulletin

The lever is not merely unaffordable; under the present AI paradigm, it may not yet exist. Smaller models that run locally remain useful, and a new architecture may offer a better path. What remains doubtful is whether today’s large language models can become superintelligent simply by feeding them ever more chips, electricity, and capital.
